en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa)
1. The First Training Rule on Confession (Pāṭidesanīya) Venerable sirs, these four matters of confession come up for recitation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhunī, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, saw a certain bhikkhu as she was returning and said to him,
“Come, venerable sir, accept some alms. “Very well,
sister,” he replied, and he accepted it all.
As the time drew near, she was unable to go for alms and her meal was cut short.
Then that bhikkhunī, on the second day as well...
and on the third day as well, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, saw that bhikkhu as she was returning and said this to him:
“Come, sister, accept almsfood.
“Very well, sister,” he replied, and they all accepted it.
As the time drew near, she was unable to go for alms; she missed her meal.
Then, on the fourth day, that bhikkhunī was walking along the carriage road, swinging her hips.
A householder merchant coming in the opposite direction in a chariot said this to her:
“Move aside, venerable lady.”
As she was stepping down, she fell right there.
The householder treasurer asked that bhikkhunī for forgiveness, saying, "Forgive me, Venerable Lady;
it was I who caused you to fall."
“I did not cause you to fall, householder;
rather, I myself was weak.
“But why, noble lady, were you weak?”
Then that bhikkhunī reported this matter to the householder merchant.
The householder merchant took that bhikkhunī to his home, fed her, and then complained, criticized, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the venerable ones accept food from the hand of a bhikkhunī?"
“Women are difficult to satisfy.
The monks heard that householder merchant as he was complaining, grumbling, and venting his displeasure.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...they complained, grumbled, and vented their displeasure:
“How indeed could a monk accept food from the hand of a nun?
… [after the usual inquiry] … “Is it true, monk, that you accepted food from the hand of a nun?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
“Bhikkhu, is she a relative of yours or not a relative?
“She is not a relative, Blessed One.
“A relative, foolish man, does not know whether it is appropriate or inappropriate, or what is real or unreal, toward one who is not a relative.”
"How indeed, foolish man, could you accept food from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule: 'If a monk should accept food from the hand of an unrelated bhikkhunī, he commits an offense of expiation.'"
“Whatever monk, having received with his own hand fresh or cooked food from the hand of an unrelated nun who has entered among the houses, should eat it or consume it, that monk must confess:
‘Friend, I have fallen into a blameworthy, unseemly offense entailing confession; I confess it.
“Whatever monk,” etc.
Whoever is such a one … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is what is intended by the term “bhikkhu” in this context.
"Non-relative" means one who is not connected by blood on the mother's side or the father's side, up to the seventh generation of ancestors.
"Bhikkhunī" means...
One who is fully ordained in both Saṅghas.
"Within a house" means a carriage road, a street, a crossroads, or a private dwelling.
"Hard food" (khādanīya) means:

setting aside the five kinds of cooked food, that which is for a watch of the night, that which is for seven days, and that which is for life—the remainder is called "hard food. "Soft food" (bhojanīya) means: [the five kinds of cooked food].
There are five kinds of food: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat.
If one receives them with the intention, "I shall chew it; I shall eat it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every swallow, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).

If, perceiving a woman who is not a relative as one who is not a relative, he receives fresh or cooked food directly from her hand when she has entered among the houses, and then eats or consumes it, he commits an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).

If, being uncertain about whether a woman who has entered among the houses is not a relative, he receives fresh or cooked food directly from her hand and then eats or consumes it, he commits an offense entailing confession.

If, perceiving a woman who is not a relative to be a relative, he receives fresh or cooked food directly from her hand as she has entered among the houses, and then eats it or consumes it, he commits an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
If he receives for the purpose of food anything that is to be used within a watch of the night, within seven days, or for life, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful swallowed, he commits an offense of wrong-doing.
If she receives fresh or cooked food from the hand of one who is fully ordained on only one side [of the Order],
thinking, "I will eat it, I will consume it," there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is a relative but one perceives her as not a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is a relative but one is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is a relative and one perceives her as a relative, there is no offense.
There is no offense:
if she is a relative;
or if she causes [another] to give, but does not give herself.
Having set it down, he gives it;
within the monastery,
in the nuns' quarters.
On a sectarian’s bed,
at the time of returning,
or having brought it out from the village, he gives it.
If one gives [food] to be consumed within a watch of the day, within seven days, or for life, with the thought,
"Use this when there is a reason," to a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerī);
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of the first offender.
The first training rule on acknowledgment is finished.
